clue.text: Gutless Swiss caught by sword remains petrified?

parts.note: a foil is a fencing sword

indicators.note: with its guts gone, SWISS keeps only its two outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of SWISS

explanation.surface: A Swiss fencer, run through by a blade, lies there stiff with fright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petrified' reads as terrified, but here it means turned to stone; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: bones or shells slowly turned to stone over millions of years.

clue.text: Acceptable target in 'Test Your Strength' or 'Hook a Duck'?

definitions.text: Acceptable target in 'Test Your Strength' or 'Hook a Duck'?

parts.note: someone it is legitimate to attack or mock

parts.words: in 'Test Your Strength' or 'Hook a Duck'?
parts.note: not a moral point: these are two sideshow amusements at a funfair

explanation.walkthrough: Test Your Strength and Hook a Duck are games at a funfair, so each is literally a fair game; FAIR GAME is also the idiom for an acceptable target.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone open to criticism or ridicule, here also read literally as sideshow amusements played at funfairs.

clue.text: Counterfeit note of debtor banked by team

indicators.note: the team sits on either side of the note, like banks around a river

parts.note: Spurs is Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club
an IOU is a written promise to repay

explanation.surface: A forged debt note turns up in a football club's bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banked' suggests money paid in, which suits a debtor's note; here it only means the team's letters flank the note.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something fake, made to pass as genuine.

clue.text: A little bonsai on Asian island

indicators.note: only a small part of the words 'bonsai on Asian' is wanted

parts.note: bonsaI ON Asian

explanation.surface: A miniature tree growing on an island in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asian' belongs to the fodder, so the island is not in Asia at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a small Scottish isle in the Inner Hebrides, famous for its abbey.

clue.text: Lovely top mark realistic, first in Russian bagged

parts.note: A is the top grade
a realistic task is doable

indicators.note: only the first letter of Russian is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Russian

explanation.surface: A teacher praises a piece of Russian homework as lovely and realistic.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the clue into two jobs: A plus DOABLE, then the R tucked inside DOABLE after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something charming and delightful to look at.

clue.text: Double jeopardy has caught people almost entirely off guard, initially

indicators.note: all of PEOPLE except its last letter is used

parts.note: jeopardy is danger
PEOPLE without its final E

indicators.note: only the first letter of guard is taken

parts.note: the first letter of guard

explanation.surface: A defendant tried twice for the same crime catches everyone off guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double jeopardy' is a legal phrase, but the two words split: 'Double' is the definition and 'jeopardy' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a ghostly or uncanny lookalike of a living person, borrowed from German.

definitions.meaning: a verb: to sway or jolt back and forth
a noun: a small smooth stone

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a verb and the second a noun; read together they look like an instruction to jiggle a stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: a verb for swaying to and fro, and a noun for a lump of stone.

parts.note: B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black
an eagle is a bird

explanation.surface: A dark bird of prey out on the hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the black bird itself the hunter; the hunter is really a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a small hound bred to chase hares by scent.

clue.text: Old rotten tree in West Country city

parts.note: ex = former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: rotten wood falls apart, so TREE comes apart and re-forms

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An ancient decaying tree stands in a city in south-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is the south-west of England: Devon, Cornwall, Somerset and nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the cathedral city and county town of Devon.

clue.text: Animal is generally undernourished, and needing affection primarily

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter of each word

parts.words: is generally undernourished, and needing affection
parts.note: Is Generally Undernourished And Needing Affection

explanation.surface: A neglected pet, underfed and in need of love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' sits at the end, so it applies to every word before it except the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a large tropical lizard, often kept as a pet.

parts.note: sage means wise
a pace is a step

explanation.surface: A modern move gets a warm reception from a wise elder.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word 'Step' opens 15 down with a different job; here it gives PACE, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: modern and up to date, named after the era of rockets and satellites.

clue.text: Let your hair down more, chaps, little time for feeling of uncertainty!

parts.note: to let your hair down more is to be wilder
chaps are men
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A plea to men to loosen up, with little time left for doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: BE WILDER is read as a command, 'be wilder', which is what letting your hair down more means.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: total confusion, the state of being baffled and not knowing what to think.

definitions.meaning: tiny particles of stone or sand

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second definition is loose: little bits of what is left unsaid.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: courage and staying power, and the coarse sand spread on icy roads.

parts.note: a revel is a lively celebration

explanation.surface: A party at the pub goes badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' reads as a pub, which suits the party; here it is a metal rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rigid rod used to prise something open or shift a load.

definitions.meaning: the steak order for meat barely seared on each side
smutty, as a crude joke or film

explanation.walkthrough: 'Very rare' reads as uncommon; it is the cooking term for a steak rarer than rare.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a steak barely cooked, and humour that is indecent or smutty.

parts.note: a luminary is a star, a leading light
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A celebrity finally catches someone out at the first step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nailed' reads as caught out; here it means the I is fixed between the letters of STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one tread in a flight leading between floors.

parts.note: a dude is a man
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Someone urges a friend to taste some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dude, try' reads as a friendly command, but each word just supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a sweet tropical stone fruit with orange flesh.

clue.text: Stuck in ditch, an outing ruined for climber

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit stuck inside the ditch

parts.note: a moat is a defensive ditch

indicators.note: a ruined outing has fallen apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A day trip spoilt when the party gets stuck in a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a person scaling rock; here it is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a sure-footed wild animal of North American cliffs and crags.

parts.note: a train that runs on a single track
a joke, and the question mark says the train is a disguise

explanation.walkthrough: A monorail train is a liner on one line, so it could be called a ONE-LINER; the gag is a joke told in a single sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a short quip, dressed up here as a single-track train.

indicators.note: the letters of ALARMING shift into new places

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Worrying changes whose merit is open to argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alarming' looks like a description of the shifts; it is the fodder, and 'shifts' is a verb telling it to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a borderline case sits so close to the line that people can argue either way.

clue.text: Name in heading dead stupid, reason kept secret

indicators.note: stupid means senseless, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: anagram fodder
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A name in a headline announces a death, stupidly, for a reason nobody reveals.
explanation.walkthrough: The N joins the letters of HEADING DEAD before they are rearranged, making twelve letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an ulterior motive someone conceals while pursuing their plans.

clue.text: Empty sheet, paper for school class

indicators.note: an emptied sheet loses its middle, keeping just S and T

parts.note: the first and last letters of sheet
a ream is 500 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: A blank sheet of paper handed out in class.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools pupils are often streamed, split into groups by ability.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British schools, a group of pupils taught together by ability level.

indicators.note: the letters of IT ON switch places

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone keen to turn a machine on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switching it on' reads as flicking a switch; 'switching' is swapping the letters of IT ON.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: you are 'into' a hobby or band you are keen on.

indicators.note: tangled fibres are jumbled, like these letters

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A short thread that has got knotted up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like it describes the fibre, but it is the definition, standing apart from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lasting little time or using few words.

definitions.meaning: a noun: a swig or gulp, often of spirits
a verb: to hit someone hard

explanation.walkthrough: Next to 'Drink', punch looks like the fruity party drink; it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a quick gulp of spirits, and slang for hitting someone hard with a fist.

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Counting the hours of a working day up to twelve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twelve' looks like a number, which 'Number' points at; here it is a time of day.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the clock time marking midday, when the hands meet at the top.

parts.note: to hug is to cuddle
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A fan embraces an elderly writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' belongs to the wordplay, though it fits the author too: he died in 1885.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Victor Hugo, the French novelist who wrote Les Misérables.

indicators.note: the letters of NAMES are changed around

parts.note: anagram fodder
an individual is one person

explanation.surface: A gardener relabels flowers with new names, one at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is only part of the answer: the container step splits it open before the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a genus of flowering plants related to buttercups, also called windflowers.

clue.text: Unknown number visiting European city retire

parts.note: Turin is a city in northern Italy
n is the algebra letter for an unknown number

explanation.surface: An anonymous number of tourists stopping in a European city before heading off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retire' suggests leaving work; here it means going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: both mean going to bed for the night.

clue.text: Party elected to punch crony, bully

parts.note: a do is a party
a crony is a mate, a friend
a candidate elected is in

explanation.surface: A newly elected party member thumps a pal, a bully in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' and 'elected' suggest politics, but a do is a social party and IN is simply what an elected candidate is.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym as verbs: to push others around and control them by force.

clue.text: Pen top on rubber in shade of pink

parts.note: coral is an orange-pink colour

indicators.note: the top of rubber is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of rubber

explanation.surface: A pencil with a pink rubber eraser on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' and 'rubber' paint a desk scene, pencil and eraser; the pen is an enclosure for animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fenced enclosure for cattle or horses, especially on an American ranch.
